Documentation is supposed to help developers. In reality, it often slows them down. Large projects ship with thousands of pages spread across API references, tutorials, and READMEs. The problem is not missing information. The problem is finding the right information at the right time.
When someone asks “How do I get started?”, they want a tutorial. When they ask “What parameters does near_text accept?”, they want a precise API reference. Traditional search treats both queries the same and returns a mixed list of links. That wastes time.
A better approach is to build a Router Agent. Instead of searching everything blindly, the agent first understands intent and then routes the query to the most suitable source.

articles.author: Genco Divrikli
articles.description:
Model drift is silently destroying your forecasts. Here's the complete guide to detecting it before it costs you millions.
Last Ramadan, a major GCC retailer lost an estimated $4.2 million in revenue. Their AI-powered demand forecasting system—which had performed flawlessly for 18 months—suddenly started recommending the wrong inventory levels. Stock-outs on essential items. Overstock on products that weren't moving.
The culprit? Model drift.
Their system had been trained on data from the previous year, but Ramadan had shifted by 11 days. Consumer behavior patterns had evolved. Post-Iftar shopping windows had changed. The model didn't know any of this. It was confidently wrong.
This isn't a hypothetical scenario. According to a comprehensive MIT/Harvard study across 128 model/dataset pairs…
articles.title: Why Your Retail AI Model Will Fail This Ramadan (And What to Do About It)

articles.author: Ankit Khandelwal
articles.description:
I bought my first 3D printer this week to make parts for the robot I'm building.
The print head moves slowly, laying down each thin line of plastic.
It is strangely calming to watch.

I keep thinking about all the little things I’ve wanted over the years like headphone stands, cable holders, desk gadgets.
shaka laka boom boom and make them real.
Friends who visit are equally fascinated.

What still surprises me is how affordable this has become.
Before buying it, I had reached out to more than 20 printing vendors to get my robot parts made.
In the end, I bought the printer for about 15k, spent around 5k on filament, another 10k on a few big parts I still outsourced, and finished everything for under 30k.
Now I keep noticing new machines that can even turn 2D photos into 3D models.
For now, though, it still feels like a niche hobby.
Most people I know have heard of 3D printing, but have never actually used it.
Someone just needs to make the whole experience a bit simpler, tell the right story, and this will explode.
articles.title: Ghibli moment for 3D Printing
